story.headline: Can a website add seats to Parliament?

reason: picked by hand; Josh's own words (headline, post, video_lines)
post:
Can a website add seats to Parliament?

Harry Mowbray, father of Zuru's billionaire founders, is pushing a campaign urging voters to give their party vote to ACT or NZ First and their electorate vote to National. Mowbray argues it would guarantee an election win.

Chris Hipkins is not a fan. "Trying to rort the electoral system to protect your own entrenched interests... is an absolute rort. I'll call it out as a rort." He also said: "You should vote for the party you want to lead the government."

It is not a one-way street. Te Pāti Māori openly seeks an overhang for the left too.

Party donations are public. Since 1 January, parties on both the left and the right have reported gifts of more than $20,000 to the Electoral Commission.

Overhangs have happened before, including in 2005, 2008, 2011 and 2023.

So, should voters be free to split their votes however they like, whoever is pushing the idea?

Political circles are also debating a quirk that could leave some top National ministers, including Paul Goldsmith, out of Parliament. He is contesting a seat ACT has held since 2005.

Tonight a Kingmakers Debate features Swarbrick, David Seymour, Winston Peters, Rawiri Waititi and Opportunity's Qiulae Wong.

The kingmakers, it seems, are already arguing over who gets the crown jewels.

article.title: Can a website add seats to Parliament?
article.excerpt:
Tactical voting has become one of the odder talking points of the campaign, and the short answer to our headline is no. No campaign, website or otherwise, can add a seat to Parliament. What it can try to do is shift which parties fill the seats that are already there.

The idea is being debated in political circles because of what it could do to some of National's senior ministers. One of them is Paul Goldsmith, who is contesting an electorate seat ACT has held since 2005. If voters in a seat like that split their two votes in particular ways, some top ministers could end up outside Parliament
